text.content:
The Status Perfectus ("Perfect State") is the closest thing the Anarch Movement has to a founding charter, analogous in weight and function to the Camarilla's Six Traditions or the Sabbat's Code of Milan — though far less binding in practice, since no central authority exists to enforce it. It was drafted by the Revolutionary Council, the body that had coordinated the anarchs' military campaign during the Second Anarch Revolt of December 1944, when a coalition led by Jeremy MacNeil and Salvador Garcia overthrew the Los Angeles princedom of Don Sebastian and carved out the Anarch Free State, a self-governing anarch territory stretching from the Mexican border to San Jose. Before dissolving itself, the Council adopted the Status Perfectus as a set of principles of self-governance for the new Free State.

What It States

Although clearly rooted in older anarch philosophies going back to the original 14th-century Anarch Revolt, the Status Perfectus was the first document to state the anarch dream clearly and unequivocally in modern times. Its core tenets:

  • Anarchs everywhere should care for one another regardless of clan affiliation.
  • Anarchs should help each other break free from the shackles of the Lextalionis (the elder-favoring law of the Camarilla and, by extension, any sect hierarchy built on generational privilege).
  • It promises a Kindred nation free of political oppression and elder prejudice.
  • It swears to extend that freedom to all Kindred everywhere, not merely to those already within the Movement.

Canon Status and Use at the Table

The Status Perfectus is aspirational rather than enforceable: it was never backed by a standing government, court, or blood hunt-equivalent sanction, and the Anarch Free State that produced it collapsed by 2000 under a combination of internal factionalism and the Cathayan Quincunx's divide-and-conquer New Promise Mandarinate scheme. Despite this, the document remains a touchstone of anarch identity and rhetoric — anarchs who invoke "the Perfectus" are appealing to the movement's highest ideals even though no one can compel another anarch to honor it. A Storyteller running an anarch chronicle can treat familiarity with the Status Perfectus (its history, its core tenets, and the Convention of Thorns it stands in defiance of) as basic anarch cultural literacy: the Anarch Free State was itself widely considered proof that the ideal was achievable, however briefly, and its fall is a live source of both cynicism and renewed resolve for modern anarchs. Notably, ignorance of the Status Perfectus's principles (along with the history of the Cause and the significance of the Convention of Thorns) is specifically called out elsewhere in anarch source material as the kind of gap that marks a character as an "Unenlightened" anarch in name only.
